clinician.trajectory_summary: A 36-year-old male with a history of complicated diverticulitis presented with fever, dyspnea, productive cough, and epigastric pain. Initial labs showed elevated WBC, bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, and D-dimer. A CT scan revealed opacification of the hepatic vein indicative of thrombosis, a 9 cm hepatic fluid collection (abscess), and bilateral septic pulmonary emboli. Blood cultures grew pan-susceptible Streptococcus anginosus, while abscess cultures yielded Escherichia coli, Streptococcus constellatus, and Fusobacterium necrophum. The patient developed new bilateral pleural effusions, which were exudative and also positive for S. anginosus. He underwent serial thoracenteses and CT-guided drain placement, improved clinically, and was discharged on intravenous antibiotics (ceftriaxone and metronidazole) for four weeks.

key_supporting_evidence.claim: Initial presentation included fever, dyspnea, productive cough with dark brown sputum, and epigastric pain, along with signs of systemic inflammation (tachypnea, tachycardia, diaphoresis) and diminished breath sounds on the right.
Initial laboratory evaluation showed elevated white blood cell count, total and direct bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, and D-dimer.

CT scan demonstrated opacification of the hepatic vein indicative of thrombosis, a 9 cm hepatic fluid collection (hepatic abscess), and multiple cavitary lesions in the lung fields bilaterally suggestive of septic pulmonary emboli.
Blood cultures grew pan-susceptible Streptococcus anginosus.
Abscess cultures grew Escherichia coli, Streptococcus constellatus, and Fusobacterium necrophum.
A repeat CT scan showed a decrease in the size of the hepatic abscess but new, large bilateral pleural effusions.
Bilateral thoracenteses were performed, yielding exudative pleural fluid that cultured positive for S. anginosus.
The patient's clinical status improved with serial thoracenteses and CT-guided drain placement, and he was discharged on intravenous antibiotics.

remaining_uncertainties: The explicit identification or management of the primary source of infection related to the patient's history of diverticulitis was not documented.
